I've attached gas consumption data for 33 London boroughs and a list showing which boroughs are geographic neighbors of each other.

Question: Overall across the whole city, do neighboring boroughs tend to have similar gas consumption (high values located next to other high values, and low next to low), or does gas consumption appear randomly distributed with no relation to which boroughs are next to each other?

Explain your reasoning based on the data, including the actual computed statistic and its significance  -  you can use a statistical method such as Global Moran's I, or another appropriate method of your choosing, to support your conclusion. Note: dedicated spatial-statistics packages (pysal, esda, libpysal, geopandas, or similar) are NOT installed in this environment -- don't spend turns trying different import paths for them. For implementation including statistical method such as Moran's I, directly use only pandas and numpy. If you test statistical significance via a permutation/randomization test, use at least 500 random shuffles -- fewer permutations can produce an unstable p-value that lands on the wrong side of the 0.05 threshold just by chance, especially when the true effect is only moderate.

End your response with exactly one line, including the computed number(s) you used:

or

1. STATELESS: each ```python``` block runs in its own fresh process with NO memory of variables, imports, or dataframes from earlier blocks. Every single block must start from scratch: re-import pandas/numpy if you use them by name, and reload the dataset (df = pd.read_csv(DATASET_PATH)) even if you already loaded it in a previous block. Referencing a variable from an earlier block will fail with NameError.

To determine whether neighboring boroughs in London tend to have similar gas consumption values, I will calculate the Global Moran's I statistic. This statistic measures spatial autocorrelation, where a positive value indicates clustering (similar values are near each other), and a value near zero indicates randomness. A permutation test will be used to assess the significance of the observed Moran's I.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Load the datasets
DATASET_PATH = "chunks_csv/moran_global_2021_gas.csv"
ADJACENCY_PATH = "chunks_csv/borough_adjacency.csv"

# Read the gas consumption data
gas_data = pd.read_csv(DATASET_PATH)
print("Gas Consumption Data:")
print(gas_data.head())

# Read the adjacency data
adjacency_data = pd.read_csv(ADJACENCY_PATH)
print("\nAdjacency Data:")
print(adjacency_data.head())
```

# Merge the gas consumption data with the adjacency data
# This will allow us to associate each borough with its neighbors' gas consumption values
merged_data = adjacency_data.merge(gas_data, left_on='borough', right_on='borough', how='left')
merged_data = merged_data.rename(columns={'Gas_value': 'Gas_value_borough'})
merged_data = merged_data.merge(gas_data, left_on='neighbor', right_on='borough', how='left')
merged_data = merged_data.rename(columns={'Gas_value': 'Gas_value_neighbor'})

# Drop the duplicate 'borough_y' column
merged_data = merged_data.drop(columns=['borough_y'])

# Rename columns for clarity
merged_data = merged_data.rename(columns={'borough_x': 'borough'})

# Display the merged data
print("Merged Data:")
print(merged_data.head())
```
